## Learning Objectives

By the end of this lesson you will be able to:

- **Describe** **multi-head attention** -- several attention heads in parallel, each with its own
  projections, concatenated -- and say why several heads beat one. *(Understand)*
- **Explain** **positional encoding**: why an order-blind set operation needs it, and how a sinusoidal
  or learned position signal injects order. *(Understand)*

  feed-forward network) and stack blocks into a working encoder. *(Apply -- in the lab)*
- **Analyze** why the Transformer is attention **plus** position **plus** residual/layer-norm blocks:
  positional encoding flips an order task from chance to solved. *(Analyze)*

  **GPT** language-model families. *(Understand)*

## Why This Matters

L21 ended on a cliffhanger. A single attention layer can reach any position in one hop -- a huge win
for long-range dependencies -- but it is **order-blind**: shuffle the input tokens and the output is
identical, because attention treats its input as a **set**. For a lookup that is fine; for language it
is fatal, since "dog bites man" and "man bites dog" would look the same.

Everything else about a Transformer is engineering around the attention you already built. Run several
attention computations in parallel (**multi-head**). Wrap each sublayer in a residual connection and a
normalization step so deep stacks stay trainable. Add a small per-position network for extra
nonlinearity. And -- the one genuinely new idea -- tell the set-based layer **where each token sits**
with **positional encoding**. Assemble those, stack the result a few times, and you have the
architecture introduced in *Attention Is All You Need* (2017) that now powers BERT, GPT, and modern
large language models.

## Multi-Head Attention

One attention computation produces one weighted blend per position -- it can track **one** kind of
relationship at a time. A sentence has many at once: agreement with the subject, the referent of a
pronoun, the boundary of a clause. **Multi-head attention** runs several attentions in **parallel**.
Split the width $d$ into $h$ **heads** of size $d/h$; give each head its own $W_q, W_k, W_v$; run
scaled dot-product attention independently in each; concatenate the $h$ outputs back to width $d$ and
mix them with a final $W_o$:

$$\text{MultiHead}(X) = \operatorname{concat}(\text{head}_1, \ldots, \text{head}_h)\, W_o, \qquad
\text{head}_i = \text{attention}(X W_q^i, X W_k^i, X W_v^i)$$

Because the heads are independent, they can **specialize** -- one head learns to look at the previous
token, another at a distant noun, another at punctuation. It costs almost nothing: $h$ heads over
$d/h$ dimensions is the same total work as one head over $d$. In the lab you build this from L21's
`attention` and see four heads attend differently to the same token; PyTorch ships it as
`nn.MultiheadAttention`.

## Positional Encoding

Attention has no built-in sense of order -- the sum over positions is the same in any arrangement. To
fix that, **add a position signal to each token embedding** before the first block, so position becomes
part of the representation. The original Transformer uses a fixed **sinusoidal** encoding: dimension by
dimension, the value is a sine or cosine of the position at a geometrically decreasing frequency,

$$PE_{(p,\,2i)} = \sin\!\left(\frac{p}{10000^{\,2i/d}}\right), \qquad
PE_{(p,\,2i+1)} = \cos\!\left(\frac{p}{10000^{\,2i/d}}\right)$$

so fast dimensions separate neighbors and slow dimensions separate far-apart positions; together they
give every position a unique fingerprint. Modern models usually **learn** the signal instead -- a
trainable `nn.Embedding(max_len, d)` indexed by position -- which works just as well. Either way, the
point is the same: no amount of depth recovers order from a set, so position must be **injected**. This
is exactly the missing ingredient L21 named.

## The Transformer Block (Add & Norm)

A Transformer is a stack of identical **blocks**. Each block has two **sublayers** -- multi-head
self-attention (mix information *between* positions) and a **position-wise feed-forward network** (a
small MLP applied to each position independently, for per-token nonlinearity) -- and wraps each one the
same way: a **residual connection** then **layer normalization**, the "Add & Norm" pattern.

$$x \leftarrow \text{LayerNorm}\big(x + \text{MultiHeadSelfAttention}(x)\big), \qquad
x \leftarrow \text{LayerNorm}\big(x + \text{FFN}(x)\big)$$

The **residual** connection is the L19 idea: add the input back, so each sublayer only learns a
*change* and gradients have a short path -- which is what lets blocks stack deep. **Layer
normalization** is new here, and worth contrasting with L17's batch-norm: layer-norm standardizes each
**token across its own features**, independent of the batch, which suits variable-length sequences far
better than batch statistics. A block maps a sequence to a same-shape sequence, so blocks stack
cleanly; `nn.TransformerEncoderLayer` is exactly this.

```{mermaid}
flowchart TB
  x["input tokens<br/>(embedding + positional encoding)"] --> a["multi-head self-attention"]
  x -- "residual" --> n1["Add and Norm"]
  a --> n1
  n1 --> f["feed-forward network<br/>(position-wise MLP)"]
  n1 -- "residual" --> n2["Add and Norm"]
  f --> n2
  n2 --> out["block output<br/>(same shape, stack again)"]
```

## Stacking into the Architecture

Stack $N$ of these blocks and you have a Transformer **encoder**: every position has gathered context
from the whole sequence, repeatedly refined. Two structural variations cover most of what you will
meet:

- A **decoder** generates a sequence left to right. Its self-attention is **masked** so a position can
  only attend to itself and earlier positions (no peeking at the future); it can also add
  **cross-attention** to look at an encoder's output.
- An **encoder-decoder** pairs the two -- the encoder reads the input (say, a French sentence), the
  decoder writes the output (the English translation) while attending to the encoder. This is the
  original 2017 design.

The whole architecture is the same block, repeated and arranged. What changes between models is mostly
**which mask** and **which half** you keep.

## Causal Masking and LLMs

The mask is the single structural difference between the two dominant model families. Add $-\infty$ to
every attention score above the diagonal and the softmax zeroes out the future, giving **causal**
(left-to-right) attention -- the lab does this in one line and sees a clean lower-triangular matrix.

- **BERT** is **encoder-only** with **no** mask: every token sees every other (bidirectional). Good
  for *understanding* a whole input at once -- classification, retrieval, tagging.
- **GPT** is **decoder-only** with a **causal** mask: each token sees only the past. Good for
  *generating* text one token at a time -- which is what chat models do.

```{mermaid}
flowchart TB
  blk["the Transformer block<br/>(multi-head attention + Add and Norm + FFN)"] --> bert["BERT<br/>encoder-only, NO mask<br/>bidirectional -- understanding"]
  blk --> gpt["GPT<br/>decoder-only, CAUSAL mask<br/>left-to-right -- generation"]
  bert --> u1["classification,<br/>retrieval, tagging"]
  gpt --> u2["text generation,<br/>chat, code"]
```

## Common Pitfalls

- **Thinking positional encoding is optional.** Without it the model is order-blind -- in the lab it
  sits at chance on a task that depends only on order. For language, position is not negotiable.
- **Confusing layer-norm with batch-norm.** Layer-norm normalizes each token across its features
  (batch-size independent); batch-norm (L17) normalizes across the batch. Transformers use layer-norm.
- **Thinking one block is the whole model.** A block is the repeating unit; a Transformer stacks
  several, with an embedding + positional encoding in front and a task head on top.
- **Confusing "multi-head" with "deeper."** Heads are **parallel** (wider attention, same depth), not
  extra layers. Depth comes from stacking blocks.
- **Assuming an encoder and a decoder are different layers.** They are the same block; the decoder just
  adds a causal mask (and optionally cross-attention).

## FAQ / Industry Reality

**"Is this really what GPT and BERT are?"** -- Yes, at the core. Real models are bigger (more blocks,
wider $d$, more heads), trained on enormous text with a tokenizer in front, and tuned heavily -- but
the block you build here is the repeating unit in all of them. The differences are scale and the mask,
not the mechanism.

**"Why feed-forward *and* attention?"** -- They do different jobs. Attention **mixes** information
across positions; the FFN **transforms** each position on its own. Alternating them -- mix, transform,
mix, transform -- is what gives the stack its expressive power.

**"How big do these get?"** -- The block is cheap, but attention's cost grows with the **square** of
the sequence length (L21), and models stack dozens to hundreds of blocks over thousands of dimensions.
That is why training frontier models takes data centers, and why long context is expensive.

**"Do Transformers only do language?"** -- No. The same architecture handles vision (Vision
Transformers split an image into patches and treat them as tokens), audio, protein sequences, and more.
Anything you can present as a sequence of tokens is fair game.

## Summary / Cheat-sheet

| Concept | The one-liner |
|---|---|
| Multi-head attention | `h` attentions in parallel over `d/h`-wide slices, concatenated -- heads specialize |
| Positional encoding | a per-position signal (sinusoidal or learned) added to embeddings -- gives order to a set |
| Residual + layer norm | "Add & Norm": add the input back (short gradient path) then normalize per token |
| Feed-forward network | a position-wise MLP -- transforms each token independently |
| Encoder block | self-attention + Add&Norm + FFN + Add&Norm; stack `N` of them |
| Decoder / causal mask | `-inf` above the diagonal -> left-to-right attention (generation) |
| BERT vs GPT | encoder-only/bidirectional (understanding) vs decoder-only/causal (generation) |
